claims.text: The alloy is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing phases with different corrosion stabilities, such as BCC- and FCC-related constituents.
The various phases initially possess intact native passive films.
The controlled intervention is sliding wear applied while the alloy is immersed in a corrosive electrolyte at elevated temperature.
The proposed operating regime is above approximately 800 K in an aggressive, potentially chloride-containing electrolyte.
Sliding wear mechanically abrades and thins the protective passive oxide layers.
Passive-film disruption occurs preferentially on the more corrosion-susceptible eutectic phases.
Film disruption establishes galvanic cells between exposed, less-protected regions and intact regions.
Compositional heterogeneity produces localized electrochemical-potential differences between phases.
Galvanic coupling between eutectic phases can cause selective anodic dissolution.
Galvanic coupling accelerates corrosion specifically at mechanically worn sites.
Increasing temperature promotes selective dissolution in the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The reported temperature dependence of selective dissolution supports extrapolation to temperatures above 800 K.
Combined wear and corrosion will produce a higher overall degradation rate than static corrosion under matched environmental conditions.
Combined exposure will produce an increased wear rate relative to the static-corrosion baseline.
Combined exposure will enhance localized corrosion relative to static corrosion.
Combined exposure will cause greater material loss and a measurable change in electrochemical impedance.
The matched baseline consists of specimens under the same temperature and electrolyte conditions but without sliding wear.
The mechanism is expected to apply only where a passive film forms under elevated-temperature, aggressive-electrolyte conditions.
EIS, polarization, wear-track measurements, and SEM/EDS can be used to distinguish film disruption, localized corrosion, and material loss between combined-exposure and static-corrosion specimens.
The hypothesis is rejected if wear causes no significant passive-film deterioration or no statistically significant increase in combined degradation relative to the control.
